medium.title: Exported activity NewPasswordActivity has no permission protection
medium.description: Activity "edu.ksu.cs.benign.NewPasswordActivity" is reachable by any app on the device (Has an intent-filter and no explicit android:exported (implicitly exported)) and declares no permission. It handles NEWPASS. NewPasswordActivity is exported and lacks permission protection, allowing any app to trigger its decryption logic via the 'edu.ksu.cs.benign.NEWPASS' action.
medium.impact: If a password reset token and IV are leaked (e.g., through logcat), any installed app can use this activity to decrypt the token and reveal the user's email address.
medium.recommendation: Set android:exported="false" if it is internal, or guard it with a signature-level permission and validate all input.

medium.title: Password reset tokens and IVs logged in ResetPasswordActivity
medium.description: The application writes sensitive password reset tokens and their corresponding initialization vectors (IVs) to the system log using Log.d. This information can be read by any application with access to logcat (on older Android versions) or via ADB, potentially allowing an attacker to intercept the reset flow.

lines_html: cipher.init(1, secretKeySpec);
java.lang.String token = android.util.Base64.encodeToString(cipher.doFinal(emailAddr.getBytes()), 0);
android.util.Log.d("Benign/ResetPassword", "Token = " + token);
android.widget.Toast.makeText(edu.ksu.cs.benign.ResetPasswordActivity.this.getApplicationContext(), "Token emailed!", 1).show();
java.lang.String initializationVector = android.util.Base64.encodeToString(cipher.getIV(), 0);
intent.putExtra("initVector", initializationVector);
android.util.Log.d("Benign/ResetPassword", "IV = " + initializationVector);

info.title: Application is debuggable in this build
info.description: android:debuggable="true" lets any user with adb attach a debugger to the process, read and modify memory, and inspect application data. The application is marked as debuggable in the manifest.
info.impact: An attacker with ADB access can attach a debugger to the process, inspect memory, and use 'run-as' to access the app's private data directory.
info.recommendation: Remove android:debuggable or set it to "false" for release builds.

reasons: Debuggable release build. A debuggable build is a release-pipeline defect rather than an exploitable flaw - attaching a debugger already requires ADB access to the device. Worth fixing, not worth a severity.

info.title: Missing screenshot protection on sensitive screens
info.description: The application does not set FLAG_SECURE on its activities.
info.impact: Sensitive information, such as the email address displayed in NewPasswordActivity, can be captured via screenshots, screen recordings, or the app switcher thumbnail.
info.recommendation: Call getWindow().setFlags(WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE, WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE) in the onCreate() of sensitive activities.

reasons: Screen contents not protected from capture. Without FLAG_SECURE, what a screen shows can end up in screenshots, screen recordings and the task-switcher preview. That matters on screens showing credentials, card numbers or balances; on its own it is a hardening note.
Screen contents not protected from capture reaches at most CVSS 3.3 (Low); the vector given scores this finding above anything the class does.

info.title: No network security config declared
info.description: The app declares neither android:networkSecurityConfig nor usesCleartextTraffic, so it relies on platform defaults and pins no domain. With targetSdkVersion 27 those defaults still permit cleartext HTTP (see the cleartext finding).
info.impact: Without pinning, anyone who gets a CA trusted on the device can read and alter the app's TLS traffic.
info.recommendation: Declare a network security config that disables cleartext and pins the domains that carry sensitive traffic.

reasons: No certificate pinning. Pinning defends against an attacker who already controls a trusted CA or the device's trust store. Without one of those, TLS is still doing its job. It becomes a finding when paired with what the unpinned channel actually carries.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 27 allows implicit component export
info.description: On targetSdk 27, any component with an intent-filter is exported unless it says otherwise.
info.recommendation: Raise targetSdkVersion to 31+ and declare android:exported explicitly on every filtered component.

reasons: Legacy platform behaviour from SDK levels. An SDK level is a statement about which platform defaults apply, not a defect. It is context for the findings that depend on those defaults - pair it with one of them.
warnings: Implicit export only applies below targetSdk 31; confirm the app's targetSdkVersion before treating this as exploitable.

info.description: targetSdk 27 predates API 28, where cleartext HTTP became opt-in.

reasons: Cleartext permitted by configuration. The flag permits HTTP; it does not show that anything is sent over it. Name a request that actually goes out in cleartext, and what it carries, and this is a genuine finding.
warnings: Cleartext is blocked by default from targetSdk 28; confirm the declared target and any network security config.

info.title: Task hijacking (StrandHogg) possible on Android 10 and lower
info.description: minSdkVersion 22 lets the app run on Android versions before 11, and its task affinity is its package name "edu.ksu.cs.benign". There, another app can declare the same affinity, with allowTaskReparenting, and have its own activity shown in this app's task. The application targets SDK 27 and does not specify a unique taskAffinity for its activities. This allows a malicious app with the same affinity to hijack the task and display a fake UI over the app's screens.
info.impact: An attacker can trick the user into entering sensitive information or performing unintended actions by overlaying a malicious activity on top of the legitimate app.
info.recommendation: Raise minSdkVersion to 30, where Android fixed this. Until then, android:taskAffinity="" on the <application> mitigates the original attack, though not its runtime variant on unpatched Android 9 and lower.
